extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of literary criticism; poets and critics studying poetic style and the function of criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for reading, judging, and writing poetry and literary criticism—definitions of important stylistic ideals (e.g., the 'grand style') and statements about the purpose of literature and criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grand style
rubrics_metrics.description: The grand style arises in poetry when a noble nature, poetically gifted, treats with simplicity or with severity a serious subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arnold admits the term 'grand style' is incapable of exact verbal definition but identifies it by this characteristic combination (see his On Translating Homer). Use this as a criterion to judge whether a poetic passage attains the 'grand' manner: look for nobility of conception and simple or severe treatment of serious themes. (Reference: footnote noting Arnold's fuller description in 'On Translating Homer'.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Literature as 'a criticism of life'
rubrics_metrics.description: The end and aim of all literature, if one considers it attentively, is, in truth, nothing but 'a criticism of life.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied especially to poetry (Arnold defends this application), this criterion treats literary work as valuable insofar as it interprets, judges, or illuminates human life and conduct. When evaluating poetry, ask whether the work offers insight into life, ethical reflection, or a 'criticism' that contributes to humane ideals. (Notes indicate Arnold's phrase and its defense in his essays.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Introductions and appreciations should be by competent critics
rubrics_metrics.description: A practice of printing a notice by a competent critic to serve as an introduction to an eminent author's works might be revived; the disciple must be also, as in this case he is, a critic, a man of letters, not... some relation or friend with no qualification for his task except affection for his author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a guideline for editorial practice and for framing readers' reception: prefatory notices or critical introductions should be written by qualified critics (people with literary competence), not by relatives or friendly admirers lacking critical qualifications. Anti-pattern: introductions written solely from affection rather than critical judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defendability and applicability of critical principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical phrases or principles (such as 'a criticism of life') may be attacked but can be defended when reasonably applied (Arnold notes the phrase was attacked when applied to poetry and defends it in his essay on Byron).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using sweeping critical maxims as evaluation tools, ensure they are appropriately and carefully applied to the specific literary form and supported by argument or exemplification. In practice, do not apply broad principles uncritically—explain and defend their relevance to the work being judged.
